source_read: PDF, Curr Opin Hematol 2012;19:27-31 (all 5 pages; text layer extracted with pdftotext -layout; every number used checked on the rendered pages pp. 27-30 at 150 dpi, including the Figure 1 and 2 captions; p. 31 is references only)

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source on numbers or causation: the claim uses 'describe', 'attributed' and 'linked', gives no rate of harm, and keeps the second-hand and unsourced labels (in this review the 73.2% sentence and the 5.6 h half-life carry no reference: confirmed on the page). Minor wording points on the claim's text: (1) the claim's 'most often after smoking' drops the review's caveat, in the same sentence, that it is unclear whether smoking crack or freebase carries a greater risk than other routes (p. 28); keep it, so the sentence is not read as a route-specific risk. (2) Urine detection for about 2 to 3 days is described as preliminary evidence, applies to most patients and is tied to how long benzoylecgonine stays detectable (p. 30). (3) The claim's 'commonest adulterant' paraphrases the review's most abundant adulterant (p. 28), which can also mean the largest quantity; the same sentence says concentrations were low (1.5-4.1%). (4) The claim's 'from hospital patients': this review says only urine samples that screened positive for cocaine metabolites (p. 28) and patients who use cocaine (p. 30); a hospital is named only in the title of the Denver reference [11]. (5) The claim's 'Case reports and small series from 2009 onward, first from Alberta ... Colorado, describe two conditions': the 2009 first reports from these places concerned agranulocytosis (p. 28); the review places the skin vasculopathy in anecdotal reports since 2009 and calls it the new finding of the past year (p. 29). (6) The review also says the vasculopathy seems much more common with cocaine-borne than with therapeutic levamisole, judged from the number of anecdotal reports without denominators (p. 29): another frequency statement without a number, which the claim could list beside the significant-minority statement.
claims.note: All numbers from this source confirmed on the rendered pages: DEA first detection 2003 [9]; 73.2% of cocaine analysed by the DEA in January 2010 (no reference; the preceding sentence, 30% of seized exhibits adulterated by 2008, cites [3], a 1999 paediatric case series of therapeutic levamisole that cannot hold 2008 data, so the review's sourcing of the seizure figures is unreliable); Luxembourg 1.5-4.1% [10]; Denver 78% and San Francisco 88% of urine samples screening positive for cocaine metabolites, published 2011 [11,12]; neutrophil recovery within 2-3 days of GCSF in most case reports and spontaneous recovery 5-10 days after exposure ended [13,14,18]; about half of the patients with more than one episode on return to cocaine use [20; Knowles 2009, the Alberta and British Columbia series, so the claim's 'one series' is right]; about half of vasculopathy cases with neutropenia [24,25,29]; lesions usually resolve within a few weeks; plasma half-life estimated population mean 5.6 h (no reference) and serum testing likely negative more than 24 h after last exposure; urine about 2-3 days [11,12]. Frequency: the only rates in the review are therapeutic-use antibody formation (0.4-20% depending on the condition treated, p. 27) and agranulocytosis in the general population (5 per million per year, p. 28); neither is a rate among people exposed through cocaine, and the claim rightly gives none. The significant-minority statement (Summary, p. 27) has no number behind it: confirmed. How cases were found and confirmed: laboratory confirmation of levamisole is mentioned for the first in-depth case (early 2010, [18]) and for one pictured patient (Figure 2 caption, urine GC/MS); otherwise the review ties cases to levamisole by cocaine history, the clinical pattern and the therapeutic-use precedent, and recommends testing only in select cases (p. 30). The claim's 'attributed ... mainly from their pattern, ... cocaine use ... and from the same effects seen when levamisole was used as a medicine' is the editors' characterization and is consistent with this review. Cocaine itself is never weighed as a cause (the review cites reports whose titles call a vasculopathy [27] and a midline destructive lesion [36] cocaine-induced among its levamisole citations, without discussion): confirmed. Leukoencephalopathy: no cocaine-acquired case reported to date (p. 30); the review adds a probable, unpublished case at the authors' institution, which the claim omits; the Purpose of review (p. 27, which says levamisole is known to cause neurologic complications), the Summary, the Key points and the Conclusion all list it, so the claim's 'although its summary lists it' is right. Medical use: this review (2012) says levamisole is FDA-approved as adjuvant chemotherapy for colon cancer but no manufacturer markets it for human use in the US (p. 27); the 2015 review says the FDA banned it in 2000. The claim's 'formerly used in people' fits both for the US. Findings only: the claim correctly leaves out the review's speculation that levamisole might enhance cocaine's euphoric effects or make it more addicting (p. 28). The clause 'so cases were often attributed without measuring it' is attributed to the later review and assessed there; this review does not support it either (it says specific testing may be unnecessary in many cases, p. 30, but does not count how many reported cases had levamisole measured).

anchors.extracted: Levamisole is a veterinary drug used mainly against worm infestations in cattle, sheep and pigs [1]; formerly used for autoimmune disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, nephrotic syndrome) and cancers (breast, lung); described as FDA-approved as adjuvant chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil for colon cancer; medicinal use common in the 1980s; no manufacturer markets it for human use in the US.

In therapeutic use, 0.4% to 20% of treated patients (depending on the condition) form isoimmune antibodies to neutrophil cell-wall antigens; agranulocytosis in the general population estimated at 5 cases per million per year [6]; levamisole used as a medicine also implicated in cutaneous vasculopathy and leukoencephalopathy [3,7,8]. No rate among people exposed through cocaine.

DEA first detected levamisole in cocaine bricks seized in trans-shipment in 2003 [9]; 30% of seized cocaine exhibits adulterated by 2008 [3]; January 2010 data: 73.2% of cocaine analysed by the DEA contained levamisole (no reference given); Luxembourg study of illicit cocaine samples: levamisole the most abundant adulterant but at low concentrations, 1.5-4.1% [10]; studies from Denver and San Francisco published in 2011: levamisole in 78% and 88% of urine samples that screened positive for cocaine metabolites [11,12]; early reports of effects in people using crack and powder cocaine, by injection, insufflation and inhalation [13,14].

First human cases of agranulocytosis with levamisole-contaminated cocaine reported in 2009 from Alberta, British Columbia, New Mexico, Washington, Arizona and Colorado [13,14]; first in-depth case report with laboratory confirmation in early 2010 [18]; most patients developed agranulocytosis after smoking cocaine, but whether smoking carries a greater risk than other routes is unclear [20]; about half of the patients had more than one episode on returning to cocaine use [20]; ANCA commonly detected (continues p. 29) [21,22].

No controlled trials of treatment for levamisole-associated agranulocytosis; most published case reports describe neutrophil recovery within 2-3 days of GCSF; older and recent reports describe spontaneous recovery 5-10 days after exposure ends [13,14,18]; the added benefit of GCSF is unclear; marrow biopsy may be deferred in neutropenic patients with a clear history of cocaine exposure.

Vasculopathy rarely reported with therapeutic levamisole but, from the number of anecdotal reports since 2009, seems much more common with cocaine-borne exposure (no denominators); purpuric plaques in a retiform or stellate pattern, with bullae, necrosis, ulcers, livedo, splinter haemorrhages [24]; typically ears, cheeks, nose and extremities [31]; cocaine use more prevalent in men (SAMHSA) but women predominate among cases [24]; on p. 30: diffusely positive autoantibodies including antineutrophil cell-wall antibodies, c- and p-ANCA, anticardiolipin, anti-dsDNA, anti-RNP, antiphospholipid [26,29]; histology pure small-vessel vasculitis, thrombotic vasculopathy or both [24,30]; about half of cases with neutropenia [24,25,29].

Treatment not well studied; stopping cocaine is the first step and lesions usually resolve within a few weeks; other treatments (corticosteroids, colchicine, phentolamine, anticoagulation, skin grafting) rest on anecdote, with little systematically collected data [24].

Therapeutic levamisole associated with a reversible multifocal inflammatory leukoencephalopathy [5,8]; no case acquired through cocaine reported to date, though the authors mention a probable, unpublished case at their institution; no data for or against the treatments advocated.

anchors.locator: Abstract, Purpose of review and Summary
anchors.extracted: Summary: more than three quarters of US people who use cocaine are exposed to levamisole and a 'significant minority' will develop neutropenia, cutaneous vascular complications and/or leukoencephalopathy (no number given); Purpose: levamisole said to be known to cause vascular and neurologic complications, although the body (p. 30) reports no cocaine-acquired leukoencephalopathy.

Given the high prevalence of exposure, specific testing may be unnecessary in many cases; GC-MS in urine and plasma; plasma half-life estimated population mean 5.6 h (no reference), so serum testing likely negative if last exposure was more than 24 h before sampling; preliminary evidence that urine stays positive as long as benzoylecgonine is detectable, about 2-3 days after exposure ends in most patients [11,12]. Conclusion (p. 30): testing in select cases.
One pictured patient with confirmed cocaine use and levamisole detected by urine GC/MS (reproduced from [31]): an example of a case in which levamisole was measured.

key_findings.correction: The Denver (78%) and San Francisco (88%) figures come from studies published in 2011; the review gives no sampling dates, so 'in 2011, levamisole was found' should read 'studies published in 2011 found'. Luxembourg: the review's term is most abundant adulterant, with low concentrations (1.5-4.1%); 'commonest' is a fair reading. Other figures (2003, 30% by 2008 with the ref. 3 problem, 73.2% unsourced) and the locator (Introduction, 5th paragraph, p. 28) confirmed.

The review says the first in-depth case report with laboratory confirmation appeared in early 2010 [18]; the card (and its 2010 timeline entry) drops 'in-depth', which turns it into a statement that no earlier report had laboratory confirmation, which the review does not make. On route, the review says it is unclear whether smoking carries a greater risk than other routes (better than 'without a clear difference in risk'). The rest (2009 first reports from the six provinces and states [13,14]; about half with repeat episodes in one series [20]) and the locator confirmed.

Two hedges dropped: the urine window (positive about as long as benzoylecgonine, about 2-3 days in most patients) is introduced as preliminary evidence, and the authors say specific testing may be unnecessary in many cases (not that it is unnecessary). Figures (5.6 h estimated population mean, no reference; serum likely negative after more than 24 h; urine 2-3 days [11,12]) and the locator confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed on the pages: 30% by 2008 cited to [3] (Rongioletti 1999, children treated with levamisole); 73.2%, the SAMHSA 5.9 million estimate and the 5.6 h half-life have no citation. The SAMHSA statement that cocaine use is more prevalent in men (p. 29) is also uncited.

'Not supported by the figures cited for it' overstates: the two urine figures (78% and 88%) do exceed three fourths and the Summary cites no figure. The problem is generalization from two local samples of urine screens to all people who use cocaine in the US (and the seizure figure, 73.2%, is below three fourths). The review does not say both samples were hospital populations: only the Denver reference title names an inner-city hospital; the San Francisco setting is not given in this review.
Ref. 31 printed as J Med Toxicol 2011;29:299-303 and ref. 18 as J Med Toxicol 2010;6:160-164 (p. 31): confirmed as printed. I did not open the project's reading list.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high: agree (no search or selection, no appraisal, mostly case reports; refs 11, 18, 31 and both figures from the first author's work). The Purpose of review also states as established that levamisole causes vascular and neurologic complications (p. 27), which supports the some-concerns judgment on separating evidence from speculation.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: agree. Two corrections to the card's 'claimed' text: (1) 'urine samples from two hospital populations' - the review names a hospital only through the Denver reference title; (4) 'most cited cases were not laboratory-confirmed' is not stated in the review, which gives no count of laboratory-confirmed cases (it mentions confirmation for the first in-depth case [18] and the patient in Figure 2); the same unsupported 'laboratory confirmation of levamisole in a minority' appears in cannot_establish. Either say the review does not report how many cases were confirmed, or anchor the proportion to the primary reports.

missed: p. 29, Cutaneous vasculopathy, 1st paragraph: the review says the vasculopathy, rarely reported with therapeutic levamisole, appears much more common with cocaine-borne exposure, judged only from the number of anecdotal reports since 2009 (no denominators). This is a second frequency statement without a number, beside the significant-minority statement, and belongs in the interpretation gap.

p. 27, Introduction, 3rd paragraph: this review (2012) says levamisole is currently FDA-approved as adjuvant chemotherapy for colon cancer (though not marketed for human use in the US), whereas Roberts 2015 (p. 1058) says the FDA banned its use in the US in 2000. A claim on levamisole's medical status should not rest on this review's statement alone.

p. 29, Neutropenia and agranulocytosis, 1st paragraph: the HLA-B27 or HLA class 1 predisposition reported for therapeutic use is said to be not replicated among patients exposed through cocaine [23]; the card's unmeasured_premorbid field says 'had not been studied', which is a stronger reading than the review gives.

p. 28, Introduction, 7th paragraph: the review speculates, from animal data and theory, that levamisole might enhance cocaine's euphoric effects or make it more addicting [16,17]. The card mentions only the reinforcement theory; any claim must keep this out of potentiation language (findings only).
